card.headline: Why you should never learn a word *alone*

beats.speech: Forgetting three out of four new words isn't laziness. It's just human memory at work.
We lose 56 percent in an hour, 66 percent in a day, and 75 percent in six days.
Learning words in isolation is the issue. Livid equals very angry without context is just noise to your brain.
Second, give it a scene. Put it in a sentence. He was livid when his flight was cancelled. Attaches a situation to a feeling, creating a solid memory anchor.

card.headline: The *synonym spin*
card.sub: One picture for each word, from mild to extreme

beats.speech: Finally, use the synonym spin so they hold each other up. Don't learn livid alone. Assign a specific picture to each synonym, mild to extreme.
Cross is a mum eyeing muddy shoes on clean carpet. Irate is a customer arguing loudly at the service desk.
Fuming is stuck in traffic, steam practically escaping your ears. Seething is sitting silent, jaw clenched, anger boiling underneath in a meeting.
Furious is slamming the door so hard the pictures shake. Livid is pale with rage when that flight is cancelled.
Incensed is reading an unfair headline and feeling absolute outrage. And apoplectic is red-faced, so angry you can't even speak.

card.headline: One word, *eight pictures*.
card.sub: cross → irate → fuming → seething → furious → livid → incensed → apoplectic

beats.speech: Remembering one picture pulls up the whole family, proving synonyms are for nuance, not decoration.

card.headline: Never learn a word *alone*.
card.sub: Look it up · grab 5 synonyms · a picture for each · anotherwordfor.net

beats.speech: So to beat the forgetting curve, never learn a word alone. Next time you look a word up, grab five of its synonyms and a picture for each in seconds at anotherwordfor.net, and tune in for episode two to find out why rereading your word list doesn't work.
